q: How do you handle missing values?
a: First understand why they're missing (MCAR, MAR, MNAR). Then: drop columns that are mostly empty and uninformative; impute median for skewed numeric, a "Missing" category for categorical; KNN or iterative imputation for MAR; always consider a missing-indicator flag; let XGBoost/LightGBM handle NaN natively. Fit imputers only on training data.

q: How do you encode a categorical feature with 5,000 levels?
a: Not one-hot. Options: smoothed target encoding computed out-of-fold; frequency encoding; grouping rare levels into "Other"; hashing; native categorical support in LightGBM/CatBoost; embeddings in a neural net. I'd usually start with CatBoost or out-of-fold target encoding.

q: Why must target encoding be done out-of-fold?
a: If a row's own label is included in its category's mean, the feature partly contains the answer. For rare categories (n = 1) it is the answer. The model looks great in CV and fails in production. Compute each row's encoding from other folds only, and add smoothing toward the global mean.
Distance or gradient based and regularised ones: KNN, K-means, SVM, PCA, linear/logistic regression with regularisation, neural networks. Not trees, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost.

Standardisation (z-score) gives mean 0, std 1; good default, keeps outliers as large values. Min-max normalisation squeezes to [0, 1]; good for bounded inputs like images or neural nets, but one outlier compresses everything else. Robust scaling uses median and IQR when outliers are present.

First decide if they're errors (fix or drop) or real extremes (keep). Detect with IQR, z-score, isolation forest. Treat by capping/winsorising, log transform, robust scaling, or using robust models/losses (trees, Huber). Never drop outliers from the test set.

q: Give an example of data leakage you've seen.
a: Example: in a loan default model, a feature "number of collection calls" was strongly predictive, but calls only happen after a customer starts missing payments, so it wouldn't exist at application time. Signs: suspiciously high AUC and one feature dominating importance. Other common ones: scaling or SMOTE before the split, random split on time data, same customer in train and test.

q: What feature selection methods do you know?
a: Filter (correlation, mutual information, chi-square, IV, variance threshold), wrapper (RFE, forward/backward selection, Boruta), embedded (L1, tree importance, SHAP-based). Also remove near-duplicates via correlation or VIF and check stability across folds.

q: How do you engineer features from a date?
a: Day of week, month, quarter, holiday flag, month-end flag, days since an event, tenure, time to next event. Cyclic sine/cosine encoding for periodic parts. For time series, lags and rolling statistics computed only from the past.

q: What is WOE and IV, and when is high IV a red flag?
a: WOE = ln(%good / %bad) per bin, which puts each bin on the log-odds scale for logistic regression. IV sums (%good − %bad) × WOE and measures predictive power. IV above about 0.5 is suspiciously strong and often signals leakage or a target-derived feature.

q: Why use log transform on a feature?
a: To reduce right skew (income, spend, counts), make relationships closer to linear, and reduce outlier influence. Use log1p for zeros; Yeo-Johnson for negatives. Trees don't need it.

q: Binning a continuous variable: pros and cons?
a: Pros: robust to outliers, captures non-linear effects in linear models, interpretable (scorecards), handles missing as a bin. Cons: loses information within bins, arbitrary boundaries, jumps at edges. Trees bin automatically, so it's mostly useful for linear models.
